title: Top 50+ most expensive rare Pokémon cards of all time
content:
What are the most expensive Pokemon cards in the world? After 30 years of regular Pokémon TCG releases, there are quite a few staggeringly valuable cards out there. YouTuber Logan Paul famously blew over $5 million on a Pikachu Illustrator in 2022 and sold it in 2026 for $16 million, but that's just the tip of the iceberg.

We've searched online auction houses and scoured Pokémon history to find the 67 most valuable rare Pokémon cards ever sold.

Because you're a true connoisseur, we know you'll want to read on for all those tasty, big money cards. But if you'd rather skip to the cream of the crop, hop straight to the top 10 most expensive Pokémon cards.

For details on how we track card sales for this guide, and expert tips on finding your own cards' value, you can also head to the FAQ section at the end of this guide.

These are the most expensive Pokémon cards:

67. Pokémon Card Fan Club Shining Magikarp

Price $14,000
Sale date May 24, 2023
Auction house Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
Grader Beckett
Rating GEM MT 9.5

Back in the early 90s, the Japanese Pokémon Card Fan Club (later succeeded by Pokémon Trainer's Card Magazine) advertised an extra-shiny Shining Magikarp promo. This fancy fish could only be won by obtaining 600 'GET points' at tournaments between 2000 and 2002.

As you can imagine, copies are fairly scarce. With so few available, it makes sense that a 9.5 gem mint copy fetched $14,000 on the auction site Fanatics Collect in 2023.

Functionally, the card is identical to Shining Magikarp from the regular 2002 Neo Genesis set. It has extremely similar art as well - you wouldn't know you had a gem at first glance.

What marks this Magikarp out from its school is the foiling. In the regular version, the background fish are shiny, whereas in the promo edition, it's the main, foreground Magikarp who shimmers. Just goes to show: when collecting rare Pokémon cards, the details matter.

66. Squirtle #29 Reverse Holo (Boundaries Crossed)

Price $15,000
Sale date March 16, 2026
Auction house Ebay
Grader PSA
Rating PSA 10

Not all rare Pokémon cards start off rare. In fact, these days, it's not uncommon to see a pretty unremarkable card sell for silly money, merely because only a few people had the foresight to preserve a copy. 10+ years later, collectors will pay above the odds for one of the only top graded copies of that card in existence.

So it is with Squirtle #29 Reverse Holo from the 2012 set Boundaries Crossed. In late 2023, PriceCharting logged the sale of a PSA10 copy for just $250. But in March 2026, one sold for a princely $15,000 on Ebay, via the PSA Vault consignment service. That's a 5,900% increase in just over two years.

Reportedly, only two confirmed PSA 10 copies of the card exist, and the firms says it's only graded 37 copies at any grade - suggesting a vanishingly small pool of collectible-quality Squirtles out there. So it's certainly rare; only time will tell if paying 15 grand for this bathing cutie was a good investment.

65. First Edition Shining Charizard

Price $15,000
Sale date October 30, 2022
Auction house Goldin
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

One of the coolest Charizard cards ever printed, Shining Charizard from 2000's Neo Destiny set features a black shiny 'zard, with a foil treatment making the Pokémon literally 'shine'. Shining Pokemon were introduced in the previous set, Neo Revelation, and were very hard to get hold of, found in one pack in every 300 on average.

That scarcity was also reflected in the game's rules too. You were limited to only having one of each Shining card in your deck.

While still a darn sight less rare than their video game equivalents, Shining Pokémon in Neo Genesis were not common, so first edition versions that have remained in mint condition are now extremely scarce. The most expensive example of the card we found was this version, sold on eBay in January 1, 2025. It was originally listed for $17,999, but tracking sites like 130point claim the final selling price was $15,000.

64. Base Set First Edition Holo Mewtwo

Price $15,000
Sale date April 16 2023
Auction house Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

For a certain generation of Pokémon fans, Mewtwo is the rare Pokémon, the rightful recipient of their Master Ball for (I probably threw mine at the first elemental bird I came across). It's unsurprising, then, that a card featuring the character would be worth something. Even more unsurprising is the fact it's the Base Set Shadowless 1st Edition Holo Mewtwo.

This card has everything - nostalgia, rarity, and a holographic background. It's also a shadowless card, meaning it was part of the first print run of the first English language Pokémon set. The most expensive copy we've seen sell is this PSA 10 copy sold via a Fanatics Collect auction in 2023.

63. Mega Charizard Y Poncho-wearing Pikachu

A rare Pokemon card depicting Pikachu wearing a cute little Poncho

Price $16,500
Sale date September 3 2026
Auction house Heritage Auctions
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

Mega Charizard Y Poncho-wearing Pikachu was one of two promo cards in a special box set released only in Japan on January 1. The contents were pretty similar to those of an elite trainer box, except of course for this utterly adorable Pikachu, dressed up like the then new Mega Charizard Y.

62. Espeon Gold Star

Price $22,100
Sale date February 2021
Auction house eBay
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

Get used to seeing the phrase 'gold star' when it comes to rare Pokémon cards. Essentially an evolution of the Shining Pokémon concept, gold star cards likewise show the alternate color 'shiny' variant of the Pokémon they depict - which is why this Espeon is green.

Few gold star Pokémon cards are ever printed - on average you'd find one in every two booster boxes, or 1/72 packs. This, and the fact they often feature gorgeous art of fan-favorite Pokémon, makes them extremely coveted.

Espeon Gold Star is a stunning example of this. Released in the promotional POP Series 5 set of 2007, this card regularly sells for thousands of dollars. A 2021 auction on eBay set the record high price of $22,100 for a PSA 10 copy.

Still, it's not the most valuable Eeveelution of that set - you'll learn more about that soon.

61. Gengar VMAX

Price $23,400
Sale date August 2026
Auction house eBay
Grader BGS
Rating Black Label 10

The alt art version of Gengar VMAX from 2021's Fusion Strike was one of the set's most sought-after chases - unsurprising given the charismatic art for the popular Pokémon - but it's the Japanese version printed in the earlier High Class Deck that's achieved higher prices. As reported on social media by TCG Collectr, in August 2026 a BGS Black Label 10 copy of the Japanese card sold for $23,400 on eBay. The grading made a huge difference to the price, since a (comparatively lowly) PSA 10 that sold around the same time went for a "mere" $2,600.

60. HG&SS Undaunted Umbreon

Price $25,000
Sale date May 04, 2026
Auction house eBay
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

Amidst all the special variants, errors cards, and promos you'll see on this list, it's kind of refreshing to have this entry, which is just a card featuring a Pokémon that people really like. Umbreon has almost as many diehard fans as Charizard. It's got a badass but cute design, it released in Gen 2 so there's plenty of nostalgia there, and it's an Eeveelution to boot.

In the modern era of the Pokémon TCG, we're pretty used to Umbreon SIRs being among a set's biggest chase cards, but it's even more true for older, rarer cards. This Umbreon, hailing from 2010's Undaunted set, sold in 2026 for $25,000 via eBay.

59. Japanese Basic No Rarity Symbol Holo Poliwrath

Price $25,015
Sale date 2020
Auction house Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

The 1996 Japanese Basic No Rarity Symbol Holo Poliwrath appeared in the original Pokémon base set, released in Japan in. Poliwrath isn't as widely popular as Charizard or Pikachu. Not quite the cutest Pokémon or the coolest, it's a bit of a sleeper in the original Pokédex. But every Pokémon is somebody's favorite.

At any rate, no collector in their right mind would turn down a PSA 10 card from the OG glory days of the Pokémon TCG. Proving our point, a 2020 auction from Fanatics Collect saw the water Pokémon sell for $25,015.

We should mention that the missing rarity symbol isn't a printing error, but a sign of authenticity. The first printings of first edition Pokémon cards in Japan lacked the symbol in the bottom corner. Japan didn't have shadowless cards, but these are essentially the equivalent.

58. 2009 Japanese Design Promo Spikey Eared Pichu

Price $25,800
Sale date June 2023
Auction house Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

In 2009, as a promotion for the movie 'Arceus and the Jewel of Life', the Japanese publishing company Shogakukan held a drawing contest for children and young teens. Contestants were asked to share artwork for Arceus or Spikey-Eared Pichu, with the winners being turned into actual Pokémon cards. This delightful floral Pichu was designed by the second-grade winner, who was around seven or eight years old at the time.

According to Dicebreaker, only 13 to 100 copies of this card are thought to exist, and only three copies of Spikey-Eared Pichu have ever been graded by PSA. It's no wonder, then, that the 2009 Japanese Design Promo 2nd Grade Winner Spikey-Eared Pichu card can fetch such a high price, with a Fanatics Collect auction reaching $25,800 in June 2023.

57. Gold Pikachu

Price $29,520
Sale date September 2021
Auction house Goldin
Rating EX 5

Nothing screams expensive like a flash of gold. And in this case, gold beats old. The Gold Pikachu Pokémon card was released in 2018, to mark the 20th anniversary of the Pokémon TCG.

Made of 11 grams of solid 24-karat gold, the card is a replica of the original Japanese Pikachu card's design, featuring a very round yellow mouse. To grab the card on release, buyers first entered a lottery, with winners given the chance to buy the limited edition card for a cool ¥216,000 ($2,000 / £1,700).

Since then, its value has risen swiftly. It sold for close to $8,000 (£5,750) in 2019, then $12,655 in 2020. Most recently, a version of the card went for a cool $29,520 in 2021. Notably, this was graded at EX 5 by PSA, so higher-priced Pikachu's are certainly possible

Although not legal in tournament play, the card came with a handy glass frame to display the artifact to visitors. You'd probably have to explain why spending nearly 30 grand on a single, unusable card was a good financial decision, though.

56. Darkrai #BW73

Price $30,000
Sale date April 27, 2026
Auction house Ebay
Grader PSA
Rating 10

These days, nothing seems to send a Pokémon card's price rocketing quite like its featured 'Mon becoming the mascot of a brand new expansion. Consequently, the reveal of new Japanese set Abyss Eye, in April 2026, sent high-rolling collectors scrambling for high graded copies of older Darkrai cards.

Top of the pile is the remarkably imposing-looking 2013 Black & White promo card Darkrai #BW73, which sold in PSA 10 for a record price of $30,000 on Ebay, in the same month Abyss Eye was unveiled.

That's a staggering markup from the previous PSA 10 sale we found just two months before - a comparatively casual $15k - and more than three times the one before that, which fetched only $8,700 in late 2025. This, for a card from 2013's Team Plasma box, which at the time retailed for 20 bucks.

55. X/Y 20th Anniversary Festa Pikachu

Price $32,250
Sale date September 3 2023
Auction house Goldin
Grader Beckett
Rating Pristine 10

While the Japanese X/Y 20th Anniversary Festa Pikachu is pretty recent as far as rare Pokémon cards go, it has a classic feel that older fans will still adore. It helps that all three Gen 1 starter Pokémon - plus the biggest icon of the IP, Pikachu - feature in its vibrant, adorable artwork.

This pricey piece of paper was given out to attendees of the 2016 Anniversary Festa in Toki Messe, Niigata, which took place to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the first-ever Pokémon game.

Its abilities aren't likely to win you tournaments, but they are pretty unique. A 120-damage attack 'Mega Thunderbolt' causes you to discard all Pikachu's energy, and the Celebration ability demands that every player clap their hands and then draw a card.

The highest-selling copy of this card was sold on March 9, 2023 via auction site Goldin. This card, given Beckett's maximum grade of 10 (Pristine) fetched $32,520 at auction.

54. Shining Mew CoroCoro Promo

Price $33,000
Sale date January 17, 2025
Auction house eBay
Grader ARS
Rating 10

Featuring a lovely, baby blue Shiny Mew, this Japanese Shining Mew CoroCoro promo card is incredibly hard to get hold of. It's one of Japan's unnumbered promo cards, which have short print runs attached to specific events like tournaments and film releases.

In this case, Shining Mew was a promo card released in the May 2001 issue of a magazine, the kids manga CoroCoro. As you might expect for a freebie given out in a children's comic, few copies survived in good nick. Which is why a version of this Japanese card sold in January 2025 for a whopping $33,000.

53. 2002 Trophy Card Neo Summer Battle Road No. 2 Trainer

Price $34,100
Sale date March 2021

Perhaps the rarest of all Pokémon cards, the 1999 Secret Super Battle No. 1 Trainer is the real deal. A promotional card awarded to finalists of the 1999 Secret Super Battle Tournament - also functioning as the entry ticket to the tournament's finals - it's said that only seven copies were made.

Six of them remain in perfect Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) Gem Mint 10 condition, with one selling for a whopping $156,000 in September 2022 via Heritage Auctions.

The holographic card features a silhouetted Mewtwo and, according to the auction house responsible for a sale in 2020, Heritage Auctions, the card's description translates to: "The Pokémon Card Game Official Tournament's champion is recognized here, and this honor is praised. By presenting this card, you may gain preferential entry into the Secret Super Battle".

15. Family Event Trophy Kangaskhan

Price $175,000
Sale date  July 2023
Auction house Heritage Auctions
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

The Family Event Trophy Kangaskhan card was given as a reward to participants of a 1998 Pokémon TCG battle tournament. This was no regular tournament, however, as each team was made up of both a parent and child, bringing some family spirit to the game. Those teams that reached a certain spot in the contest's ladder were rewarded this trophy card.

Let's hope they hung onto it. The card was never printed outside of the tournament, and features the original Pocket Monsters Trading Card Game logo as a set symbol (instead of the regular Pokémon TCG logo), making it quite the rarity.

Collector's seem to think so, too. In October 2020, a PSA 10 'gem mint' copy of the card was auctioned for $150,100 (£109,350) on eBay, making it one of the most expensive Pokémon cards to sell in recent years. That price was beaten in a Heritage Auctions sale in July 2023 however, setting a new highest price of $175,000.

14. 2005 Play Promo Holo Umbreon

Price $180,00
Sale date February 22 2024
Auction house Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
Grader Beckett
Rating GEM MT 9.5

The 2005 Play Promo Holo Umbreon card was only awarded to members of the Pokémon Player's Club, and they'd need to earn 70,000 EXP points (through various activities and competitions) to get their hands on a copy. Considering members start out with only 1,000 points, catching this one was no small feat.  It's one of the most notoriously difficult Player's Club promo cards to acquire.

This alone makes this Umbreon rare and desirable, but there's more: the holo version of the card was never released in English. Combine that with adorable art of a beloved Eeveelution, and you're talking real value. In a 2021 Fanatics Collect auction, this Pokémon card sold for $70,000 (£55,700) - that's one dollar for every EXP point it's worth.

But this was smashed in September 2023, when a GEM MT 10 copy of the card sold for $135,209 - followed swiftly by another sale for $180,000 in February 2024 via Fanatics Collect.

13. Test Print Gold Border Blastoise

Price $216,000
Sale date July 24, 2021
Auction House Heritage Auctions
Grader CGC
Rating 6.5

When Wizards of the Coast first attempted to localize the Pokémon card game for the English language market, they experimented with a variety of different layouts before settling on the final version. This Test Print Gold Border Blastoise has a bunch of strange features. Its back is a Magic: the Gathering card, the border is gold rather than yellow, and the front of the card is foiled, a new technique for Wizards of the Coast at the time.

12. Ishihara GX Promo

Price $247,230
Sale date 25 April 2021
Auction house Goldin
Grader PSA
Rating NM 7

A little different from the others on this list, the Ishihara GX Promo card doesn't actually feature a Pokémon, but the president and founder of The Pokémon Company, Tsunekazu Ishihara.

The promotional card was printed to celebrate his 60th birthday, and handed to the company employees who attended the event  - quite the corporate treat, given how valuable it then became.

The card's 'Red Chanchanko' ability is a reference to the traditional Japanese garment often given to men when they turn 60 years old.

Copies of the card have sold at auction for as much as $50,000 (£36,450), but that's peanuts compared to what a signed copy can fetch. In April 2021, an autographed PSA 7 Ishihara GX Promo card went for $247,230 (£180,200). It's unlikely we'll see many more of these pop up, though. It's rumored that only a handful were ever printed, and only one signed copy has ever been shown to the public.

11. Pokémon Snap Contest Pikachu

Price $270,000
Sale date June 2023
Auction house Private sale
Grader PSA
Rating Authenticated

Just like the Snap Magikarp, the Pokémon Snap Contest Pikachu was created as a promo prize for one of ten competition winners, featuring a virtual Pikachu photograph taken inside the strange photography / safari videogame Pokémon Snap. 20 copies were given to a single prize winner in the late '90s, but never surfaced on the open market.

That was until June 2023, when Pro Retro X published the video above, showing two collectors hunting down a copy of the card at Japanese TCG and sneaker marketplace Magi, and purchasing it for an eye-watering $270,000.

10. Trophy Pikachu No. 3 Trainer

Price $324,000
Sale date 24 April 2023
Auction house Heritage Auctions
Grader PSA
Rating NM / M 8

One of the most expensive prize cards on our list comes all the way from June 1997, less than one year into the Pokémon TCG's lifespan. This was the very first Pokémon tournament, and it looked very different to modern competitive play. According to the 'museum' website Pokumon, the competitors were 1,000 children (aged up to 15) chosen by lottery. Since skill wasn't required to compete, the power level was really low, with all sorts of wild and wacky decks showing up.

The first ever prize cards, each featuring different Pikachu pics, were awarded to the winners, with the No. 3 Trainer Cards given to third and fourth place competitors in each of the four tournaments. When we first wrote this guide only four of the Trophy Pikachu No. 3 Trainer cards had been PSA certified, but as of February 2025 all eight copies were accounted for.

How much does this slice of Pokémon history cost? In April 2023, a copy sold on Heritage Auctions for $300,000 and before that, one went on Fanatics Collect for $324,000. A pricey Pika!

9. Signed Japanese First Edition Base Set Holo Charizard

Price $324,000
Sale date April 16 2022
Auction house Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10
Released two years before the English language version of Pokémon, the Japanese base set has its own first edition indicator - there's no rarity symbol in the bottom-right corner of the card. A GEM MT 10 copy of the Japanese Base Set Holo Charizard, in a case signed by artist Mitsuhiro Arita, sold for $324,000 on April 16 2022. The fact that only seven copies of the card have a Gem MT 10 grading no doubt helps its value!

8. Presentation Blastoise

Price $360,000
Sale date  January 14 2021
Auction house Heritage Auctions
Grader CGC
Rating  NM 8.5

Presentation Blastoise was briefly the most expensive Pokémon card ever sold, when it went for $360,000 (£260,000) at auction in January 2021. This is no normal card: Presentation Blastoise was originally printed by Wizards of the Coast as a demonstration piece for its pitch to Nintendo to get the rights to make an English language version of the card game.

Because it's a prototype, this card features different fonts, a missing water energy symbol, and misspellings - oddities which only makes the card more prized. Presentation Blastoise has a place at the center of the Pokémon TCG's history. Only two were ever produced, one of which may be lost forever

7. Trophy Pikachu No. 2 Trainer

Price $444,000
Sale date  July 9 2023
Auction house Goldin
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

The Trophy Pikachu No. 2 Trainer was given to second place winners at the first two Pokémon tournaments ever, in 1997 and 1998. It features an illustration by card artist Mitsuhiro Arita of a happy Pikachu holding a trophy.

On September 7 2023, a copy of this card from the second (1998) tournament, known as Lizardon Mega Battle or Charizard Mega Battle, sold for an outstanding $444,000 on auction site Goldin. Weirdly, the only difference between the prize cards is that those from the second tournament have a line specifying they're from the first ever Pokémon tournament. A heinous lie! The second tournament was on a much larger scale than the first, as Pokémania began to take root.

Only 15 copies of the card were made, and only four examples of the card have survived to become PSA graded. The real clincher that makes this copy so valuable is that this is currently the only copy to have achieved the perfect PSA 10 rating. Presumably 11 cards are lying crumpled in a drawer somewhere, their owners none the wiser.

6. Topsun Blue Back Charizard

Price $493,230
Sale date January 2021
Auction house Goldin
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

The Topsun Charizard Blue Back is truly one of the weirdest cards on this list - partly because it isn't technically a Pokémon card as we know them. It features Charizard on the front and has all the right text, but this pick isn't actually part of the official Pokémon TCG. Before Creatures Inc. developed the version of the trading card game we've come to know, Topsun gave it a go, and printed a few prototype cards.

This is one of them, and not just any one of them. Its blue back and unnumbered printing make it even more scarce. Rumored to have originally been distributed in packets of gum in Japan in 1997, despite being printed with a 1995 trademark date.

As you might expect, there's not many of these left lying about; only 31, according to trading card authenticator PSA's last count.

That's why in January 2021, a PSA 10 version of the blue-backed, unnumbered, Topsun Charizard card sold for a mega $493,230 (£392,325) at auction. It just goes to show, even unofficial products can be gold for some.

5. Prerelease Raichu

Price $550,000
Sale date September 2025
Auction house Heritage
Grader PSA
Rating EX-MT 6

Prerelease Raichu looks fairly innocuous: a base set Raichu with a prerelease stamp, similar to that found on the prerelease Clefable given out as a prize at early Wizards of the Coast events. But Raichu was never given out as a prize card - in fact it shouldn't really exist, and for many years it was dismissed as an urban legend.

We've got a separate article that explains the full history, and how it came to light. Here's the short version. In 1999 when WotC was getting ready to make the prerelease Clefable card, the initial version of the print sheet contained a small number of base set Raichus as well as the Clefables. The error was caught during production proofing and corrected, so only a tiny number of the Raichus were ever made, either eight or eleven according to different versions of the story.

All the copies of the card went home with Wizards of the Coast employees, who held onto them and occasionally teased fans by showing them off at public events. It wasn't until 2006 that they were confirmed to exist, and not until 2023 until any of the cards were graded. And so far as we know, a 2025 sale of one of the cards for $550,000 is the only time they've ever changed hands!

4. First Edition Base Set Holo Charizard

Price $700,000
Sale date  2026
Auction house Private
Grader TAG
Rating GEM MT 10

Ah, First Edition Base Set Holo Charizard. Ask a casual fan what the most sought-after Pokémon card is, and there's a good chance they'll answer: first edition shadowless Charizard. Perennially popular since its release in 1999, holographic Charizards have been a staple on the wish lists of collectors and fans for over 20 years, and a legend of playgrounds everywhere.

The first edition holo Charizard is particularly valued for its age, limited availability, and the recognizable image of one of Pokémon's much-loved mascots. Like all first edition Pokémon cards, this card is shadowless, printed without the dark border on the frame that was added later. There are a very few shadowless cards that aren't first edition, but it's the combination of the shadowless border and first edition logo that's the real certification of excellence.

In October 2020, a PSA 10 mint condition first-edition shadowless holographic Charizard was bought by ex-rapper Logic at auction for a sizeable $220,000 (£173,000), only to be surpassed a month later when another Charizard of the same specifications sold for $295,000 (£210,000).

A mint PSA 10 copy sold in 2022 for $420,000 (£334,000) via Fanatic Collect (formerly PWCC Marketplace) - but in April 2026, Collectr reported a private sale from Benjamin Be to Thiago Nigro for $700,000. That makes the First edition Charizard, once again, the most expensive playable Pokémon card in the world.

3. Trophy Pikachu No.3 Trainer

Price $1,769,000
Sale date May 18, 2026
Auction house Goldin
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

It might feel odd for the third prize Trophy Pikachu card from the Pokémon TCG's earliest Japanese tournaments to sell for four times as much as the second prize card did in 2023. That's especially true, given both cards had the same perfect PSA 10 grading, both have a similar, vanishingly small population of PSA graded cards, and both were the only PSA 10 copy known to be in existence at the time of sale.

But that's exactly what happened: in May 2026, New Jersey auctioneers Goldin (yes, the ones from TV) sold the single confirmed Trophy Pikachu No.3 Trainer for a winning bid of $1.45 million - totalling 1,769,000 bucks after a 22% buyer premium. Why the huge price difference? Maybe the buyer liked the adorably tiny trophy; maybe the bronze sparkly finish simply looks a bit more like the gold of the No. 1 trophy card below.

Or maybe, in between 2023 and 2026, Pokémon cards have begun attracting so much more attention from the ultra-wealthy that the very rarest specimens are now a fashionable status symbol for billionaires (or those who wish to appear to be billionaires) to flaunt at each other.

Maybe the top end of this is mostly an ego playground for fabulously rich men who'll happily spend $1.77m - the cost of 4.1 million meals for starving people, according to the World Food Programme - on a 2.5 by 3.5 inch rectangle of cardboard, just because they can. Does it bring them as much joy as it brought a Japanese teenager at the end of one triumphant weekend in the late 90s? We can only imagine.

2. Trophy Pikachu No. 1 Trainer

Price $3,000,000
Sale date September 12, 2025
Auction house eBay
Grader PSA
Rating MINT 9

Sitting right at the top of the Trophy Pikachu Tree, fittingly, is 1998's Trophy Pikachu No.1 Trainer - extremely limited promos handed only to the winning Pokémon players at the TCG's second-ever sanctioned tournament, the 1997-98 Japanese Lizardon Mega Battle Pokémon competition.

Just like its promo prize siblings, the number-one Pikachu was illustrated by Mitsuhiro Arita. This time, the world's most popular Pokémon is lifting a trophy in the air, grinning in triumph.

Supposedly, there are only 14 copies of this card, period. We've seen others sell for thousands upon thousands, but none have quite matched the price of the copy sold in September 2025. It's understandable - MINT 9 might be the best grading we've ever seen this promo get. No.1 Trainer Pikachu is a true winner, indeed.

1. Pikachu Illustrator

Price $16,492,000
Sale date February 16, 2026
Auction house Goldin
Grader PSA
Rating GEM MT 10

The new holy grail of the TCG, Pikachu Illustrator is a promo Pokémon card originally handed out to winners of a 1998 illustration competition run through Japanese magazine CoroCoro. Only 39 copies were ever created.

It's the only card to feature the 'Illustrator' title instead of 'Trainer'. The artwork was drawn by esteemed Pokémon illustrator Atsuko Nishida, creator of Pokémon's main mascot, Pikachu. There's even a unique pen icon in the bottom-right corner, seen on no other card.

It's unknown exactly how many Pikachu Illustrator cards are still in existence, but ten PSA certified copies have been graded as 'mint'. From January 2021 onwards, it was the most expensive Pokémon card to ever be sold at auction, with a PSA 9 Mint condition card selling for a whopping $233,000 (£167,600).

Though it lost the title briefly, in July 2021 Logan Paul (yeah, that guy) spent $4 million on the only existing PSA 10 version of the card, getting the purchase accredited by Guinness World Records as the most expensive Pokémon card ever sold. But the value of the card was actually even higher: to secure the trade, Paul also handed over a lesser PSA 9 version of the card, which he'd previously purchased for $1,275,000.

The saga of this card doesn't end there. In early 2026, Mr Paul went on to sell the card to one AJ Scaramucci, once again getting Guinness involved. That's because the sales figure this time was a frankly staggering $16,492,000.

We should add that Logan also parted ways with the diamond-encrusted necklace he'd been carrying the card around in (does a $1 card taped to a $2 million car cost $2,000,001?) But even so, it's more than fair to call this the most expensive Pokémon card of all time!

It's a pity it's so rare: Pikachu looks even cuter than usual holding an oversized fountain pen.

Bonus - Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack

Price $2,700
Sale date Unverified
Auction house eBay
Rating N/A

We're including a bonus curiosity because it's just too interesting not to mention. When Wizards of the Coast realized they had accidentally printed too many Base Set booster packs branded with the first-edition logo, they covered the errant symbol with a small black triangle. A simple attempt to avoid wasting resources has generated a much-prized collector's item, as fans now clamor for a rare Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack.

It's the packaging itself that's valuable here, not the cards inside, so don't go cracking one of these black triangle packs open if you happen to find one sitting in the back of a drawer (you lucky devil).

They're occasionally found in standard Base Set booster boxes - so if you have one you'll have to weigh up whether to gamble on the chance discovery of one of the black triangle booster packs, or whether it's best to leave the box unopened for its pristine value. Some of the black triangle boosters have fetched over $2,700 (£2,000) on eBay, depending upon their condition and which Pokémon is displayed on their cover.

Rare Pokémon cards FAQ

How we find the most expensive Pokémon cards

To compile this list, we come back each month to trawl the latest sales on global trading card and collectibles auction houses like Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC), Heritage Auctions, and Goldin Auctions. We aim to keep the rankings and prices as up to date as possible.

Remember that, like all collectibles and investments, the Pokémon card market is very volatile, and prices can change fast and often. If you're looking to buy and sell high value Pokémon cards, you need to take care to double check the latest prices, being very conscious of the website or auction house's commission rates and fees.

Which Pokémon cards are rarest?

The most valuable Pokémon cards normally command high prices because they're old and there are very few copies in circulation. Most originate from the earliest Pokémon sets, or are one-off tournament prize cards printed in very low numbers. First edition Pokémon cards, peculiar misprints, and desirable old promos all fetch very high prices.

How to tell if a Pokémon card is rare?

Wargamer has a dedicated guide to Pokémon card rarity covering the basic rarity levels of cards you can open in any pack. If you think an old card you've gotten hold of could be particularly valuable, our guides to first edition Pokémon cards and shadowless Pokémon cards will help you to identify them. It's also worth referring to our guide to fake Pokémon cards, as there are plenty of counterfeits on the market.

How to sell rare Pokémon cards

We have a dedicated guide on how to sell Pokémon cards, so we recommend you read that if you're considering trading - but here's the short version.

If you think you're holding a truly valuable Pokémon card, your first port of call is to get it protected by placing it in a thin, soft-plastic sleeve, then into a protective, hard-plastic 'toploader' case. Before spending any more money on the card, it's usually a good idea to show it to an expert in-person, to get their opinion on its condition and potential value. A specialist at your local games store may be able to help.

Then you should get it graded by a well-regarded, expert grading service - PSA Pokémon card grading is the most popular in the USA. Once you get the card back with an official grading from 1 to 10, and stored in a professional PSA protective case, you should have a good idea what price range you're likely to get for it.

Bear in mind that there's usually a huge difference in value between a PSA grade 7, 8, or 9 card (generally mint condition to the naked eye) and a perfect PSA 10 card (absolutely faultless, even when viewed under a microscope from every angle). The really high prices paid by top level collectors are only for PSA 10 cards, and a PSA 10 is very often worth more than twice as much as the exact same card at PSA grade 8 or 9.

If you don't find any ultra-valuable Pokémon cards in your collection, it's really not the end of the world. This is a game, remember - what you have got is a delightful collection to treasure and play with. If you want to share any new pack pulls or treasured classics with a community of fellow fans, you're most welcome in the Wargamer Discord!

To keep up to date with the latest news about new rare cards and any bargains we find, subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter.

title: Building a Modular City, Part 3 of 3: Bigger, Taller, Dumber
content:
This three part series shows how to create a vertiginous cityfight table for Warhammer 40,000 using a combination of handmade paving tiles and modular plastic terrain kits. Whether you like scratch building or painting plastic kits, there’s something here for anyone keen on terrain. In this third part: big centrepiece ruins in the Sector Imperialis, and how to add urban rubble to your terrain pieces.
  • Post one: carving paving tiles for the buildings to sit on.
  • Post two: modular, stackable ruins built with the Sanctum Administratus kit.
  • Post three: demonstrating techniques for creating rubble on some big centerpiece buildings.

If after the previous post any doubts lingered as to the budgetary ‘wisdom’ of the path I am walking down, this final post will surely offer some conclusions. The brain worms had a vision, and my friends and I have doggedly pursued that vision over several years, storage consequences be damned. So here we are, the finale: some big honking Sector Imperialis ruins. Waxing lyrical about these kits is fairly pointless, given that they are not currently something you can buy, so this post will primarily provide guidance on how to add rubble to any urban terrain you might have, should the urge take you.

An Enthusiastic Rant: Terrain Rules are More Like Guidelines

One might reasonably wonder where these buildings fit into the newest edition of Warhammer 40K, with those recommended terrain layouts full of little ruined Ls and random lengths of pipe, but I'm not concerned with that. Models last far longer than editions of 40K. My priority will always be to make cool terrain and then think about how best to use it in the current rules. Under no circumstances will I alter pieces of terrain I already own to conform to the preset terrain areas of 11th edition, because they will only be relevant for the next three years. The mission deck itself has guidance for placing terrain if you’re not using one of the recommended layouts, and even then, it’s not like Games Workshop are going to police the terrain you set down on your gaming table. So have fun with it and make something that looks cool while also offering interesting gameplay. After all, if you always stick with the official layouts, you'll never get to have any verticality on your table. Real height quite literally adds a third dimension to a battle, and really lets flying units shine.

The upcoming terrain sets look very well executed, and I'm glad that it's possible to play a viable game of 40K without having to embark in the sort of absurd project we're talking about here. I'm all for making the game more accessible. But the terrain below, while great for some dusty frontier town, won't give me the feeling of defending/despoiling an Imperial city.

Warhammer 40,000 Battlefields: Armageddon. Credit: Games Workshop. Used without permission for illustrative purposes only.

The Joys of a Group Effort

When Games Workshop put the Sector Imperialis kits on Made to Order, it immediately spawned another group project among the four most terrain-juiced members of my gaming group. Our main desire was to have a bloody great big archway, and then… whatever else we could build with what we bought. Which was quite a lot. We already have terrain that can provide smaller more sensible ruins, so the priority was some big-ass buildings to give a sense of scale, and open up the possibility of more vertical gameplay. Working as a group enabled us to spend more, and pool our building and painting efforts. Terrain is a communal good, made far easier by communal effort.

The Necessary Compromises of Scale

With multiple large buildings to do, the methods employed to apply rubble and paint needed to be as simple as possible. Games Workshop terrain kits are often absurdly detailed, making painting every element prohibitively time consuming. A key part of the planning process is therefore deciding what you’re NOT going to do. We noticed that even in some of GW’s own publications, they often just keep the terrain painting very simple, all the better to fade into the background. So that’s what we did.

Rubble’s tricky too. It should be made of the same stuff as the building itself: absurdly over-detailed plastic components, plus dust. But even for a maniac like me that’s not entirely practical, so one has to compromise. I settled for having some half-buried plastic components, but the rest is a mix of materials that hopefully evoke urban rubble without being perfectly accurate. This made the process a lot less time consuming, at the cost of fidelity. I suspect if I’d cast up more plaster to shatter (see later) this method would enable higher fidelity, but I’m happy enough with the compromise we’ve ended up with, not least of which because models can for the most part stand upright without difficulty.

The Step-by-Step Process

Build Your Buildings

I don't think you need extra guidance from me about how to build a plastic kit, but for clarity: you'll want to have them built but not painted in preparation for making the rubble, which will be a messy affair.

Making the Rubble

We arrive now at the meat of this article: the steps used to add a rubble base to plastic ruins. This method will broadly also work with non-plastic terrain (e.g. 3D printed) but obviously you'll be using alternative adhesives for the few places where I used poly cement/plastic glue.

Phase 1: Gather Materials

You'll need the following:

  • Modelling compound. I'm using Geek Gaming Scenics' modelling compound. The compound is essential for adding bulk to your rubble!
  • 1mm thick styrene sheeting - this will form an armature for your base, so make sure you've got enough to cover the whole of the area you need!
    • Get a sanding block and use sandpaper on the styrene sheets on one side. This will improve glue adhesion, both for PVA and also for poly cement.
  • Some spare plastic sprue, trimmed flat on one side (this will be used to reinforce the styrene sheeting and provide extra grip for the modelling compound).
  • Smashed plaster (i.e. cast up a slab/sheet of plaster up to 5mm thick and then smash/break it into smaller chunks). This works better than coarse sand and small rocks, since it snaps with sharp angles, and consequently looks like smashed concrete rather than more natural-looking rocks. Alternatively you could use torn up chunks of cork sheeting; it won't look quite as good but requires less prep.
  • Spare plastic terrain components (or in my case, some leftover bitz from the terrain kit itself).
  • Various grades of sand/grit.
  • Plenty of glue sticks for your hot glue gun (this will be used to glue your bitz and rubble down).
  • Texture paint (a convenient way of patching up any booboos/gaps you notice late in the process).
  • Greaseproof paper/baking parchment. Hot glue (and most other things) can't stick to this stuff, so it's a useful work surface to slap down on your table.

Phase 2: Groundwork

Rough up the styrene. Prepare your 1mm thick styrene sheeting by sanding it on one side to improve glue adhesion. Why 1mm you ask? Surely thicker would be better? Don't worry, we're adding structural strength later on, but we want the edge of the base to be nice and thin so it doesn't draw too much attention to itself.

Draw your base shape. Draw the shape you want on the sanded side of the sheet (pencil works fine). Assuming you're gluing the building onto this base, plonk the building down on top of the styrene sheet(s). In my case, there was some extra considerations:

  • The rubble needed to be no wider than one paving tile across, to ensure buildings could remain sensibly close together, and the rubble wouldn't protrude into the road, which is 2mm lower than the pavement/sidewalk.
  • My buildings were so large that widening them with bases would've made it impossible to fit them in the storage boxes, so some of my bases got stuck on, but most of it was made to be detachable, which adds a lot of faff - so avoid this if storage is no issue! It does at least mean that if the rubble is somehow in the way, it can be picked up.
Drawing the outline of a removable rubble section onto the styrene sheet. Credit: Charlie Brassley

Cut out the base. Cut out the shape by scoring the line with a hobby knife, then bending the styrene back and forth along the line so that it snaps. Because the sheet is only 1mm thick it's remarkably easy to score and snap even wiggly/jagged lines, which is good, because you don't want the shape of the rubble to look too regular!

Stick to the building. (If applicable): Use poly cement/plastic glue to affix the building to its base. You want to use poly cement due to the strength of the join, and it's not brittle like superglue/CA glue. You can also reinforce this join with hot glue if desired.

Reinforce the base with sprue.

  • Trim some lengths of sprue so that it’s completely flat on one side.
  • Attach the sprue to the sanded side of the styrene to reinforce it. Use poly cement (plastic glue) to ensure a strong bond.
Add large plastic rubble sections. If you want to attach any plastic components to the lowest layer of the base, particularly to further disguise the edge of the base, now’s the time. If you have good contact area, poly cement is perfect. If you don't, use the hot glue gun, since the glue gun can fill the space between the pieces and the base.

A removable rubble section, partway through the process. It's been reinforced with sprue, which will help give the compound more to grip onto. Note the added plastic components, and the broken plaster affixed with hot glue. The glue used to affix the rubble also helps firm up the structure. In this photo, the rubble is up against the building it will sit next to so that I could check how well the rubble was concealing the join. Credit: Charlie Brassley

Compound application. Apply modelling compound to the base to give it volume, tapering down to a point at the edge of the base. This step provides the overwhelming bulk of the rubble. While it’s wet you can also submerge components into it and blend them in.

Tip: Keep testing usability. During this and later stages it's worth having an (unpainted, un-precious) model around so that you can check it's possible for minis to stand upright on most or all of the rubble.

Post-compound application; you can see how some larger plastic components have been half-buried/blended in with the compound. More texture will be added later to blend things in further. Credit: Charlie Brassley

The compound will take a looooooong time to try - several days - but it doesn't have to be completely dry for you to move on to the next stage. I sped things up a little by leaving them to bake in the sun on a warm concrete slab, and resumed work the next day.

Removable rubble sections now covered in compound and left out to dry in the sun. Credit: Charlie Brassley

Phase 3: Applying Texture & Rubble to the Basing

  • Dribble neat PVA (US: white/Elmer’s) glue onto your base; spread it out with a brush to cover the whole base.
  • Sprinkle coarse sand and (if available) tiny chunks broken plaster over the glue.
  • Sprinkle fine sand or grit onto the glue. The finer the sand, the better.
  • Sprinkle a few more bits of coarser stuff here and there on top of the fine sand/grit.
  • Mix PVA glue with water, pour it into a trigger spray bottle, and drown, I mean DROWN, your terrain in watered down PVA. A 1:1 ratio of water:glue is reasonable. This will soak through the sand and grit into the compound below, and lock everything together. It should also seal any plaster you’ve used.
  • Wait three years for it to dry.
The basing texture right after getting drowned in thinned PVA. Note how the sand/grit has been used to further blend in the bigger chunks of rubble. Credit: Charlie Brassley

Painting

This article isn’t really a painting article, but I’ll include this for the curious. Owing to the enormity of the buildings, this was kept as simple as possible. First, the metal walkways and railings were primed Color Forge Hyrax Brown and masked off. Any dark brown spray, or even black, would do fine.

Claims that my masking process is an absolute bodge-fest will be met with... acceptance. This was me taping some paper down to cover some bigger chunks of the balcony to save on tape and foil. Credit: Charlie Brassley

Everything was then primed with Mechanicus Standard Grey, followed by a patchy but generous zenithal spray of Zandri Dust. This will transform the look of your terrain from "a horrible mess" to "starting to look cool." You could just prime with Zandri Dust, but I like the addition of some tonal variation.

The smallest of the ruins, post-priming. Credit: Charlie Brassley

The back of the archway post-priming. Credit: Charlie Brassley

The actual painting:
  • All over drybrush with Army Painter Skeleton Bone
  • All metal fixtures except doors painted with Cygor Brown Contrast
    • This is the longest, most punishing stage; we tried not to pick out too much and assumed much of the building to be painted to match the plaster, but there's no getting around moving parts like fans, and we wanted to blend the balconies into our Sector Mechanicus walkways.
  • All metal fixtures drybrushed with Army Painter Gunmetal
  • All metal fixtures drybrushed with Vallejo Air Steel
  • Cabling picked out in Black Templar Contrast
  • Doors sloshed with Nihilakh Oxide
  • Doors lightly drybrushed with Warplock Bronze
  • Doors lightly drybrushed with Hashut Copper
  • We also picked out one or two details like sunken barrels/crates in various colours, drybrushing those colours into the rubble to create fades and preserve the dusty colour.

The End Result: My Tiny Soldiers Now Feel Tinier

So ultimately here’s where the whole thing comes together: the paving, the stackable sanctum, the Mechanicus stuff, and these big ruins. As with so many three dimensional miniature projects it’s very hard to convey what it’s like to stand in front of these terrain pieces in person, the sense of scale they give. It feels like fighting the kind of battles I slathered over in the pages of White Dwarf as a kid. They truly live up to the phrase I always come back to: terrain is the Titan you use in every game.

Loading...

Large Sector Imperialis ruin. Termagant for scale. Credit: Charlie Brassley

The removable rubble in action. Credit: Charlie Brassley

Sector Mechanicus railings will clip onto walkways without the need for glue, enabling the gantry access points to be converted into balconies. Credit: Charlie Brassley

All three of the large Sector Imperialis ruins (plus a completely flattened ruin made from spare bits). Credit: Charlie Brassley

Warhammer 40K Cityfight table. Thanks to the linked walkways it's possible for an infantry squad to move almost the whole length of the table without ever once touching the ground. Credit: Charlie Brassley

A Cityfight table layout experimenting with stacking the modular Sanctum Administratus to have walkways running on different levels. Credit: Charlie Brassley

You Can't Possibly Want More Photos

That's probably enough photos of that... but if it isn't, and you want to see even more about how this board came together, I documented the process over the years on the Beard Bunker in the Urban Board Project Log. If you want photos of the big buildings and how the gantries work, then this post in particular is the one you want.

Okay, Those Are Large, But Are They Annoying to Game on?

Compared to the new terrain specifically designed to be as easy as possible to game on? Almost certainly. You're trading in convenience and speed for cinematics and grandeur. That said, having now played a few games of 11th edition, I've found the game works perfectly well on more narrative terrain like this so long as you've got the right number of objective buildings. The archway, since it's technically two 3x4 footprints at ground level, actually works rather well as two central objectives. It also functions as most of a Kill Team board, which... tee hee.

The important thing here is that if you're not playing a tournament, you can do whatever you like. The rules will, broadly, support that. I rather like having terrain so tall that the Plunging Fire rule has to be modified; we've already encountered situations where models on the top floor should have been eligible to get the bonus because they were firing down onto models that were themselves five inches off the ground!

One would assume there are now sufficient buildings for my table, but I still have the whole Hivestorm terrain set to build, and those comparatively small buildings will help put these large boys in scale. At least I have learned how to make rubble for them. For now, I'm off to fight battles on gantries as the gods of sci fi demand.

Cobalt Scions Terminators battle Bad Moon Orks for control of vital infrastructure. Credit: Charlie Brassley Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@goonhammer.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.

title: Haunted Mouse is a pun-derful board game, but it struggles to stand out
content:
Our Verdict

Haunted Mouse is easily the cutest game I've reviewed this year. It's also a chilled, consistent, and generally delightful card game. It's worth the low price of entry, but some inelegant rules mean it may struggle to stand out in a competitive board game space.

Pros
  • Adorable theme
  • Smooth, chilled gameplay
Cons
  • Some clunky rules
  • Somehow TOO balanced

Card-shedding board games face fierce competition these days. 2019's Scout has long held its place on our best board games list, but enthralling newcomers like DNUP threaten to shake up the status quo. At the same time, party games like Things in Rings have shot to similar success.

With all this innovation, I fear Haunted Mouse might get lost in the noise. Haunted Mouse is adorable, consistent, and quietly delightful, but it doesn't successfully push design boundaries. That means it's in serious danger of being overlooked.

Published by Bezier Games, Haunted Mouse is designed by Jonathan Cox (Acorns, Mutation, Spring Cleaning). The pun-filled title should give you an idea of how much whimsy is packed in this little box. You'll play as mice suffering from (presumably, cheese-induced) nightmares.

Bad dreams manifest as a hand of cards. Different predators represent the suits you'll wrangle, and the goal is to be rid of them. Empty your hand first, and you'll earn the biggest wedge of the cheese wheel in the morning. Haunted Mouse plays over several nights, ending when a mouse completes their cheese wheel.

It's a twee concept that, thanks to Sai Beppu's adorable artwork, gives me major cuteness aggression. Your player board depicts a unique mouse named after a kind of cheese. Those dairy slices you collect are 3D pieces that slot nicely into said board. Haunted Mouse is colorful and tactile in all the right ways.

Despite appearances, this isn't a child-friendly title. The recommended age is 14 and up, because Haunted Mouse gets granular with its mechanics.

Like Scout, Haunted Mouse doesn't allow you to rearrange the cards you're dealt. You can place a card in your 'Bait' zone before a round begins, but otherwise, you get what you get.

To shed cards, you'll need to play a meld. That's either a set or a run. The first meld plays is the lead, and all following hands must beat it, either by playing more cards or ones with higher values. So far, so trick-taking-adjacent.

Haunted Mouse throws a few extra rules in. These help it differentiate itself from staples like Scout and DNUP. They also up the play time to, at most, 45 minutes - significantly longer than its most popular rivals. They also, unfortunately, make initial games a much clunkier teach.

Unique rule number one: if you want to change the type of meld you're playing, it must contain one more card than the current lead. Three nines isn't going to beat a 3-4-5 unless you have a fourth nine to sweeten the deal. This one takes a little getting used to, but every card shedder has details like these. You'll be over the hill after a round or two.

Unique rule two: your meld can only ever have one more card than the previous meld. A set of four nines is useless to you if the current lead only has two cards. This stops anyone going out in a blaze of glory with an explosive hand. It's more fair, but it's less fun for its lack of drama. It also makes Haunted Mouse a significantly slower game than its competitors, with a runtime of up to 45 minutes.

The game attempts to inject more excitement with unique rule three: Setting Traps. These are powerful hands made of four identical cards of different suits or a four-card, 'straight flush' run in the same suit. You can play them regardless of how large the current meld is, and they get discarded immediately. You then get to take another turn, placing a new lead meld.

Traps take pretty careful planning to pull off, but you're helped by unique rule four. Here's where that Bait zone comes into play.

Everyone has one or more face-up Bait cards, and there's a single Public Bait card available. As long as you use at least one card from your own hand or Bait, you can include as many of these other Bait cards in your meld. It's flexibility at the cost of helping opponents shed cards - because you need an empty hand and Bait to wake your mouse.

Haunted Mouse's unchanging hand of cards is already a challenge to explain to less experienced gamers (God knows I've faced that trial many times with Scout). All these additional rules make things slightly too complex for a game this strategically simple.

Thankfully, once everyone at the table has picked up what you're putting down, games are smooth and speedy. There's enough decisions to mull, but the lack of explosive turns make the race relaxing rather than cutthroat. 45 minutes never feels too long, even with the max player count of five.

It's cute, smart, and plenty replayable. Haunted Mouse is a $30 game that's well worth the price of entry. Sadly, I expect it'll get massively overshadowed in the end-of-year 'best of' roundups. Games like DNUP are just as new and shiny, but they're simpler, cleaner, and more elegant.

Want to talk more about this year's hottest board games? You can keep up with our reviews - and share your thoughts on them - in the Wargamer Discord.

A review copy of Haunted Mouse was provided by the publisher.

What is the YuGiOh Master Duel banlist?

The Master Duel card pool doesn't look quite the same as the one from the physical trading card game, so a separate banlist is needed to keep things balanced. Despite this, the Master Duel banlist follows roughly the same rules as the regular YuGiOh banlist.

By this, we mean there are three degrees of 'ban' a card can be subject to:

  • Forbidden - Can't be used in the Main Deck, Extra Deck, or Side Deck
  • Limited, Limited 1 - Can only have one copy in the Main Deck, Extra Deck, and Side Deck
  • Semi-limited, Limited 2 - Can have two copies max in the Main Deck, Extra Deck, and Side Deck combined

If a card is not on the banlist at all, it's referred to as Unlimited.

And that's it for the Master Duel banlist as it stands! For more on trading card games, here's all you need to know about the MTG banlist.

title: "None of us are edgy 14 year olds" - Trench Crusade's Graham McNeill on why the wargame is more than just grimdark
content:
Trench Crusade is a divisive setting. From its origins as a personal project for concept artist Mike Franchina to draw wild ideas he'd never get away with in his dayjob, it's a visceral, blasphemous setting that blends medieval history, mechanised warfare, and the kind of freaky imagery you only find in the album art for black metal bands. I've seen some people accuse the creatives making Trench Crusade of only caring about shock value: I interviewed Graham McNeill, veteran Warhammer 40k novelist and the lead author for Trench Crusade's recent Carcass Front two player campaign set, to see what he had to say.

McNeill is a veteran author and world-builder. His career has included stints as a Warhammer 40k designer, as a 40k and Horus Heresy novelist, and as lore master for Riot Games and the League of Legends universe. His work on Carcass Front for Trench Crusade is superlative, so good that I dedicated an entire article to praising it a week before I published my 10/10 review for the set itself. If I wasn't quite frothing when he agreed to an interview, I was at least peachy keen.

"Just writing grimdark for the sake of grimdark and being edgy, for want of a better term, it never feels that interesting to me", McNeill says. "None of us are edgy 14 year olds trying for shock value: if there's a [moment of] blood and guts or terror, it's for something, it's to have a proper emotional impact".

He does allow that sometimes the emotion he's trying to elicit is "Holy shit, that's messed up!" But he says the team writing Trench Crusade "want to run that gamut of emotions of horror, of triumph, of excitement, of despair". In large part that's because as much as Trench Crusade is a horror story, it's also a war story.

McNeill puts himself into the shoes of the characters stuck in the mud and mire of the setting. "There's the little tiny bit of hope left at the end that everything we're doing, maybe it can make a difference. Maybe not for us. Maybe not for generations to come. But the minute we stop fighting is when it's all over". He expands: "even if there is no chance of winning in this larger war, we still have to fight because that's what people of honor do, what people of duty do, even in the face of insurmountable odds".

I can see how that's a useful anchor point for creating characters. What motivates people to fight on in the worst circumstances? What informs their decisions? Sometimes it'll be negative emotions like spite and hatred; sometimes it'll be madness; but nobility, duty, and self-sacrifice are all powerful motivators.

The world of Trench Crusade is one that its residents still want to fight for. "As wracked with war as it is, there are places that are not as horrible", he says. "It's a dark world, there's privation everywhere because of the war and so on, but there is still life". And if "people are still living, being born, loving, living their lives", for McNeill, "even just a microscopic sliver of it in your stories allows them to be more than just grimdark misery porn".

We discussed a lot of other topics, but those will have to wait for a future article. If you want to talk about the strengths and weaknesses of grimdark fiction, come and hang out with the crew in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Pathfinder Beginner Box: Secrets of the Unlit Star Review
content:
Howdy everyone and welcome to a review of the Pathfinder Second Edition Beginner Box: Secrets of the Unlit Star! It is designed to provide a fairly complete starter package for the TTRPG curious, and comes with everything you need to run your first few sessions, along with a sample adventure, the titular Secrets of the Unllit Star.

Before continuing, we would like to thank Pathfinder publisher Paizo for providing a copy of this box for review.

Secrets of the Unlit Star Box - Pathfinder Second Edition. Image Credit: Peri

Contents

The box, as mentioned above, contains all the essentials to run both the included adventure and a variety of goodies on top of that. You get two rulebooks, one for everyone and one for the Game Master specifically, a large double sided map for the included adventure, a set of 4 pre-generated characters and 6 blank sheets to make your own characters using the included character creation rules, a set of 4 quick reference cards that provide a great summation of basic actions, rules, and conditions, a huge heap of cardboard standees (containing all the pre-generated characters, every possibly ancestry and class combination, and both the monsters contained within the starting adventure and, surprisingly to me, quite a few extra monsters on top of that!), and, finally, a set of standard polyhedral dice which I personally find oddly appealing. The colors are very pleasant and the text is huge, bright, and readable. As someone with a long-standing hatred of difficult to read, darkly colored dice, this is hugely appreciated.

Secrets of the Unlit Star box contents. Look at those dice, those are some really edible looking dice, I love them. Credit: Peri

This is a solid amount of assorted RPG components, and there is enough here to cover quite a few sessions. Nothing feels cheap, and it all packs up nicely. This is very much a box targeted at those without pre-existing collections of RPG stuff, and I mean that in a good way.

I am particularly happy with the decision to go for standees over miniatures in a starter product like this. Miniatures are nice, but painting them is an entire other hobby and you tend to get far fewer of them for the cost. The ability to run a wider range of encounters for less cost is very much appreciated, and they pack up much tighter, reducing the amount of things you need to haul to the local game shop or store on a shelf.

Hero’s Handbook

The rules included in the Hero’s Handbook cover a limited slice of the overall Pathfinder Second Edition ruleset. The character rules cover 5 ancestries (Human, Orc, Elf, Halfling, Dwarf) and 4 Classes (Bard, Monk, Sorcerer, and Barbarian), a small scattering of the game’s many feats, and leveling rules to cover levels 1-3. The rest of the rulebook covers the core player facing systems of Pathfinder Second Edition. In addition, a small choose your own adventure style solo adventure is included, which is much appreciated. 

The rules are competently laid out and presented, with clear and easy to understand language throughout. I am a particularly huge fan of the character creation summary. The lettering of where to look on your sheet for a given value or score is used consistently throughout the book. The dice are color coded every time they appear, which helps hugely when you are introducing players who have never played RPGs. Being able to consistently say “The D20 is the red one” whenever a player asks which to roll is nice and as someone who has introduced a lot of new players to this game I am actively embarrassed that I never thought of doing this myself. 

The included pre-generated character sheets came with these nice art splash pages in small booklets, something I had never seen before, but that was very nice! Credit: Peri

The included classes are all fairly easy to understand, with decent diversity in roles and gameplay styles. The Bard is a support-focused generalist, the Sorcerer fights at range with powerful magic, the Monk is fast and makes a lot of attacks, and the Barbarian is tough and hits people really, really hard. These classes roughly map onto the classic “Fighter, Mage, Thief, Priest” ISO standard RPG party, though I do personally find it a bit odd that they didn’t just include the actual Fighter, Wizard, Rogue, and Cleric classes. Considering the classic fantasy theming in both the available ancestries and the included adventure I would have expected those classic classes, but this isn’t an actual issue, just an interesting note.

I think that the extremely limited character creation rules and options are a strength of this box on the whole though, as the full Pathfinder Second Edition character building ruleset can be extremely overwhelming, particularly to new players. The more things you have to pick through before you can start playing, the higher your chances of either doing something wrong or giving up on it before you start. It is also helpful for the GM to know exactly what they are working with when it comes to party capabilities, and having those limited options means you don’t need to keep too many things in mind at any given time.

Game Master’s Guide

The Game Masters Guide covers all of the non-player facing rules, monster statblocks, a small amount of lore on Ustalav and the town of Grayce, and the included adventure module. I’ll cover the adventure module, Secrets of the Unlit Star, in its own section below. 

To start off, the rules layout and language remains clear and usable throughout this book. I didn’t see a single rule or bit of text that caused me any confusion during my initial read through. I am an experienced GM, but even setting that aside I don’t think anything in here would cause any real problems for a new GM. Considering the width and depth of Pathfinder as a game system, that is a difficult thing to have pulled off. I only had to check the book a handful of times while running the included adventure, and referencing it was easy and clear.

The best part of this whole book though, in my opinion, is the general Game Mastering advice section included towards the start that covers what you should do to start a session, tips on how to organize games, notes on breaks and how to minimize distractions, a section on making sure that one player isn’t hogging the spotlight and to make sure to split your attention evenly, and a range of other concise and very helpful game mastering advice. This section is short at only a couple pages, but 10 year old me could have really used it back in the day. As this is a product targeted at those who have never played RPGs before, this section is going to be very valuable in avoiding some of the common pitfalls that new GMs can run into. While a lot of other RPGs have a “What is an RPG and how do you run one” section, this is one of the most concise and clear I have read, and the overwhelming majority of it is applicable to any game. 

I also want to shout out the amount of quick-reference material provided in this book. The back cover has summations of the most common sorts of checks and rolls, the order of a turn, how you make an attack roll or a save, what cover does, and a few common traits that different sorts of rolls and attacks can have. On the inside of the back cover are other things you will want to reference, though these you will need a bit less often. I particularly appreciate the chart of “What knowledge skill do I roll to identify this monster”, as I have seen that trip up a lot of newer GMs.

The book also has a brief section on designing your own adventures, with both system specific and generic advice on how to construct them. There is a bit of a focus on dungeons in this section, but the advice is good and having a clear list of what your “Budget” is for monsters to construct a reasonable encounter for your players is very much appreciated. Encounter design tends to trip up new GMs, so I appreciate having this section here for those who don’t want to run the included adventure module. I have many horror stories I could share of monsters I intended to be an easy filler fight nearly killing my entire party, and these rules should help new GMs avoid that.

Speaking of monsters, there is a miniature Beasterie included in this book, with nice art for each monster and a concise statblock. The only complaint I have with this section of the book is that I would have loved to have seen something akin to the “Tactics” section that some of the 1st edition Adventure Paths had, calling out what the goal of the monsters is in a fight. When you are new to a given RPG system it can be difficult to intuit how you are supposed to use a given monster statblock, so the omission is notable. That said, whenever monsters appear in the included adventure module, they typically have combat tactics listed, so this is only a problem if you want to run things other than said included adventure module.

Overall I am particularly fond of this book. While most of the book is devoted to the included module or to system specific rules and rolls, those advice sections will help you out no matter what you go on to play, and there were a couple of things in there that were useful even to me with my 18-ish years of experience running games (namely the statement that knowledge skills should be rolled by the GM and the result kept secret from the players, only giving them what their character thinks they can remember without the player knowing if they rolled a 1 or a 20. I had genuinely never thought of that and I am a bit embarrassed about it).

Secrets of the Unlit Star

On to the included adventure module! As a warning, I will be spoiling this adventure a bit here, so if you are interested in this from the player side of things I would skip this section and just know that it's a pretty solid, straightforward starter adventure that your GM will have an easy time running.

I ran this with a group of varying levels of experience. While all had played RPGs before, only one player had any familiarity with Pathfinder 2E as a system. Secrets of the Unlit star is a classic fantasy dungeon crawl, a sunken subterranean temple corrupted by an evil priest full of undead, weird magical creatures, foul gnomes, and a central puzzle mechanic built around finding the various pieces of the titular Unlit Star, a magical artefact MacGuffin. The actual plot of this adventure isn’t particularly likely to surprise you or your players, the Villain is an evil Shadow Priest who wants to take the MacGuffin and use it to do evil shadow priest things. This can be comforting though, and if you are playing with the sorts of extremely new groups that the box is aimed at they won’t have seen this plot before, and vanilla can be a nice flavor even if you are more experienced.

Our brave heroes battle several loathsome Giant Centipedes in what will likely be many player's first RPG combat ever. Credit: Peri

The encounters here cover a wide range of the game’s rules, and the way they are presented I find very interesting. Most of the encounters on the first floor are tutorializing a given aspect of Pathfinder’s ruleset, with a very clear focus. The first fight teaches you and the players how to roll attacks, the second one teaches you about ranged combat, difficult terrain, and movement, the third is about special monster abilities, the fourth covers resistances and immunities, there is an encounter that teaches you about NPC spellcasters, things like that. I have never seen a “starter” adventure module do this sort of “Video Game Tutorial” style structure, and I genuinely really enjoy it. The nature of this module as a pure dungeon crawl helps with that, as the writers could set a specific order for those first few encounters that they would know with 100% certainty which ones you would do in what order.

Despite the nature of the adventure as a pure dungeon crawl, there are still a couple of social encounters, one with the ghost of a dead elf and another with a fungus creature that wants to sell the party things. Said fungus creature is a fun way to replenish your party’s resources, selling some healing items and other magical junk. The module also suggests a couple of opportunities for roleplaying between player characters, though this is, overall, not a particularly social or intrigue centric adventure. That straightforwardness is likely a good thing though considering the new player focus of this box on the whole, and the provided roleplaying opportunities are likely enough to get your players started and accustomed to the concept. 

My only actual structural issue with this adventure module is that the Barbarian pre-constructed character, Amiri, had a tendency when we played through this to just delete entire encounters in 1-2 turns. Some of this was dice luck, but some of the rest of it was just that a lot of the earlier encounters in this module have low HP pools that a Barbarian with a big weapon can fairly consistently deplete in a single attack due to all the bonus damage from Rage. This isn’t really that major of an issue in the grand scheme of things and we still had a great time, but it is something that I did note while playing.

Overall I quite like this module, it ran smoothly and was a nice palette cleanser as a more experienced GM. It can be a lot of fun to run some very classic dungeon crawl-y heroic fantasy from time to time, but I wouldn't recommend buying this entire box just for this adventure. It's a great pairing with all the other contents of the box and it will work pretty well as a first adventure, but it isn’t the sort of thing I would run for a more experienced party who are just new to Pathfinder 2E as a system.

Final Thoughts

In conclusion I highly recommend this box if you are new to roleplaying games as a whole. It has some solid advice, good gameplay aids, and a solid, easy to run first adventure. 10 year old me would have loved the hell out of this box. If you are a more experienced GM and are just curious about Pathfinder 2E as a system, my recommendation comes with a few caveats. A lot of the more general-use RPG things in this box are likely to be things you already have, and if you can stomach the full ruleset you are likely better off with a copy of the core rulebooks and a module of your choice. That said, if you want to dip your toes in for a lower buy-in than all of those books, this is still a solid purchase and will let you know after a couple of sessions if you want to continue with Pathfinder 2E. If your players are more experienced, I would recommend using the rules in this box to design your own adventure, or to build on top of the included module to add a bit more complexity and difficulty.
